passage:
"Maria Didi, where are you putting Nani's glasses?"
"On the shelf, Akash. They'll get broken on the chair."
"But Nani went to the market. She saw them on the chair."
"Yes. So when she comes back, where will she look?"
"On the chair!" Akash laughed. "But they're not there!"
"Why will she look there?"
"Because she didn't see you move them. She thinks they're still on the chair."
"Good thinking. Let's tell her when she's home."

qa.q: Where did Maria put Nani's glasses?
qa.a: She put them on the shelf so they would not get broken on the chair.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about working out where Nani will look?
qa.a: Akash is amused, laughing because Nani didn't see Maria move the glasses and still believes they are on the chair.

qa.q: What did Maria do that helped Akash understand?
qa.a: She asked questions like "Where will she look?" and let Akash explain the reason without help.

qa.q: How might Nani feel if nobody told her about the move?
qa.a: She might be puzzled and worried when she finds the chair empty, so telling her saves her a scare.

grounding: A child works out that his grandmother still believes her glasses are where she left them.

passage: Observation note, Class KG-B. During puppet time I put a ball in the blue box while Bunny puppet watched, then sent Bunny away. Teddy moved the ball to the red box. I asked, "Where will Bunny look?" Hafsa jumped up: "Blue box! Bunny didn't see Teddy." Two classmates said red. Hafsa explained, "But Bunny wasn't here!" 👏 Tomorrow I'll let Hafsa run the puppets so others can guess and explain their answers. — Saurabh Sir

qa.q: Which box did Teddy move the ball to?
qa.a: Teddy moved the ball to the red box.

qa.q: How can you tell Hafsa felt confident about the answer?
qa.a: Hafsa jumped up to answer and kept explaining, "But Bunny wasn't here!" even when two classmates said red.

qa.q: How could the teacher support the classmates who said red?
qa.a: Letting Hafsa run the puppets and asking children to explain their guesses gives them another turn to notice who saw what.

qa.q: How might the two classmates see Hafsa's answer at first?
qa.a: They might think Hafsa is wrong, because they know the ball is in the red box and have not yet thought about what Bunny saw.

grounding: A teacher notes a child predicting that a puppet will act on an out-of-date belief.

passage: In the afternoon heat, Reena's goat wandered from the shed to the shade by the well. Reena watched her lie down. Soon Harish Bhaiya came up the lane with his school bag. "I'll give Chhoti her water in the shed," he said, picking up the bucket. Reena covered her mouth and giggled. "Bhaiya thinks she's in the shed!" she told Amma. "He didn't see her go." Then she ran after him. "Bhaiya, she's by the well!"

qa.q: Where did the goat go to lie down?
qa.a: She wandered from the shed to the shade by the well.

qa.q: Why did Reena giggle when Harish picked up the bucket?
qa.a: She was amused that he believed the goat was in the shed when she knew it wasn't.

qa.q: What choice did Reena make that was kind?
qa.a: After enjoying the joke, she ran after him to tell him the truth so he would not carry the bucket to an empty shed.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when he hears where Chhoti is?
qa.a: He would probably be relieved to save a trip and maybe amused that his little sister knew more than him this time.

grounding: A small-town girl realises her brother holds a mistaken belief about where the goat is.

passage: In a Johannesburg kitchen, Zanele watched Jin put his orange in the blue lunchbox and go out to wash his hands. Zanele's gogo, smiling, moved the orange into the fridge. 'When Jin comes back,' Gogo asked, 'where will he look?' Zanele giggled. 'In the blue box!' 'But the orange is in the fridge.' 'Yes, but Jin didn't see. He thinks it's still there.' She ran to meet him at the door.

qa.q: Where did Jin first put his orange?
qa.a: He put it in the blue lunchbox.

qa.q: Why did Zanele say Jin would look in the blue box?
qa.a: She understood that Jin did not see the orange being moved, so he would still believe it was in the box.

qa.q: How could Gogo keep this little game kind to Jin?
qa.a: She could make sure Jin gets his orange quickly and let the children laugh about the trick together, so no one feels fooled.

qa.q: What might Jin feel when he opens an empty lunchbox?
qa.a: He might feel surprised or confused for a moment, since his belief about the orange was wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a child understanding that someone else can hold a mistaken belief, set in South Africa.

passage: At the school activity room, Ganga Ma'am shook a crayon box. It rattled. 'What's inside, Hafsa?' 'Crayons!' Ma'am opened it. Pebbles! Hafsa laughed. 'Now,' said Ma'am, 'Didi from the next class is coming. What will she think is inside?' Hafsa bit her lip. 'Pebbles?' She paused and looked at the box again. 'No, wait. Crayons! She'll think crayons, because it's a crayon box. Only we know.'

qa.q: What was really inside the crayon box?
qa.a: Pebbles were inside the crayon box.

qa.q: How can you tell Hafsa was thinking hard before changing her answer?
qa.a: She bit her lip, paused and looked at the box again, seeming unsure, before realising that Didi would believe it held crayons.

qa.q: What could Ganga Ma'am ask next to deepen Hafsa's thinking?
qa.a: She could ask why Didi would think crayons, so Hafsa explains in her own words that Didi has not seen inside.

qa.q: How might Didi from the next class react when she sees the pebbles?
qa.a: She would likely be surprised, just as Hafsa was at first, because her belief would be wrong too.

grounding: Shows a child realising another person will hold a false belief based on what they have seen.

passage: I'm Dolma, from next door. On Saturday I was in Imran's kitchen when he finished the last two biscuits from the round tin and put the lid back on. He's five. Then he whispered to me, grinning, "Abbu will open it and think there are biscuits!" He waited by the door for his father. When Abbu opened the tin and said, "Arre, empty?", Imran burst out laughing. I'm not sure what he felt, but he looked very pleased with himself.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Imran finish?
qa.a: The last two biscuits.

qa.q: What does Imran's grin and whisper suggest?
qa.a: He was excited and amused, because he knew his father would believe the tin was still full.

qa.q: How could Imran's father use this moment?
qa.a: Play along, then talk about it: "You knew I didn't know!", and remind him to tell when the biscuits run out.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Imran's reaction?
qa.a: Dolma thinks he looked very pleased with himself, but is careful not to claim to know what he felt.

grounding: Shows a young child understanding that his father will wrongly believe a tin still holds biscuits, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday: While his cousin Bittu was in the bathroom, Aparna moved the toy cars from the shelf to the basket. "Where will Bittu look?" she asked. "In the basket," said Naveen, four, pointing. Wednesday: they played again. Naveen opened his mouth, stopped, and said, "Um… the shelf? No, basket." Saturday: when Bittu went out, Aparna moved the cars again. Naveen shouted, "The shelf! Because Bittu didn't see you!"

qa.q: Where did Aparna move the toy cars from and to?
qa.a: From the shelf to the basket.

qa.q: What does Naveen stopping and saying "Um" on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: He was unsure and torn between what he knew and what Bittu knew, as the idea was just forming.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen reach the answer by Saturday?
qa.a: Playing the same game on several days, so he could keep trying without being corrected harshly.

qa.q: What would change if Bittu had watched Aparna move the cars?
qa.a: Then the basket would be the right answer, because Bittu would know where the cars are.

grounding: Shows a child coming to understand over a week that his cousin will believe the cars are where he last saw them.

passage: The rain started just as school ended. Jyoti, five, stood under the gate's shelter with her big brother Kiran, who had brought the umbrella from home that morning without telling anyone. "Mumma will look by the door for the umbrella," Jyoti said, "but it isn't there. She'll think it's lost." "So?" said Kiran. "So she'll be worried," Jyoti said. "Call her." Kiran rang from the watchman's phone.

qa.q: Who had brought the umbrella from home that morning?
qa.a: Her big brother Kiran.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti want Kiran to call Mumma?
qa.a: She was worried Mumma would look by the door, not find it, and feel upset thinking it was lost.

qa.q: What could Kiran do next time he takes something from home?
qa.a: Tell someone before he leaves, so nobody is left looking for it.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel when Kiran calls?
qa.a: Relieved that the umbrella isn't lost and glad the children thought of her.

grounding: Shows a young child understanding that her mother will wrongly think the umbrella is by the door and may think it lost.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Dadi hid the laddoo box in the top cupboard and went for her bath. Mohit, seven, moved it to the fridge. "Where will Dadi look?" he asked Sangeeta, five, grinning. Sangeeta thought hard. "In the fridge?" Then she stopped. "No. Dadi didn't see you. She'll look in the cupboard." When Dadi came back, she opened the cupboard, frowned, and said, "Who stole my laddoos?" Sangeeta giggled. "I knew it!"

qa.q: Where did Mohit move the laddoo box?
qa.a: To the fridge.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Dadi opened the cupboard?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt delighted and proud, giggling because her prediction was right.

qa.q: How could Mohit play more games like this with Sangeeta?
qa.a: He could move things while someone is out of the room and ask where they'll look, letting her explain why.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel finding the cupboard empty?
qa.a: Dadi was probably puzzled and a bit annoyed, then likely amused at the trick.

grounding: A five-year-old works out that her grandmother will look where she left the sweets, not where they were moved.

passage:
"Yogesh will think it's sweets!" Yusuf, five, shook the Eid mithai box. Inside were crayons.
"Why?" asked Ammi.
"Because it's a sweet box. He doesn't know I put crayons."
"And what do you think is inside?"
"Crayons! I know!"
Yogesh arrived. Yusuf held out the box. "What's in here?"
"Mithai!" Yogesh grabbed it and opened it. "Crayons?"
Yusuf fell over laughing. "I tricked you! You thought sweets!"
Yogesh laughed too. "Now I'll trick you."

qa.q: What was inside the mithai box?
qa.a: Crayons.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling as he fell over laughing?
qa.a: Yusuf felt gleeful and proud that his trick worked.

qa.q: How did Ammi's questions help Yusuf's thinking?
qa.a: They made him say why Yogesh would believe something different from what Yusuf knew.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel when he opens the box?
qa.a: Yogesh was surprised and maybe a little disappointed, then amused and eager to trick back.

grounding: At Eid, a five-year-old predicts that his friend will wrongly believe a sweet box holds sweets.

passage: Teacher's note, Holi week. We did the puppet story. Monu the monkey puts his ball in the red basket and goes out to play with colours. While he's away, Chiku the cat moves it to the blue box. I asked, "Where will Monu look?" Most of the class said "blue box". Pankaj (5) said, "Red basket. He didn't see Chiku." Then he added, "He'll be sad." He's getting it. I'll give him the next puppet to lead on Friday. — Deepika Ma'am

qa.q: Where did Monu put his ball?
qa.a: In the red basket.

qa.q: What does Pankaj adding 'He'll be sad' show about his understanding?
qa.a: Pankaj understands Monu's mistaken belief and imagines the puppet feeling sad and disappointed.

qa.q: How is Deepika Ma'am building on Pankaj's understanding?
qa.a: She is giving him the next puppet to lead on Friday, so he can practise explaining others' beliefs.

qa.q: How might the other children see Pankaj's answer?
qa.a: Some might be puzzled at first, having said 'blue box', and curious to hear why he chose the red basket.

grounding: A teacher's Holi-week note records a five-year-old passing a puppet false-belief story.

passage:
On Eid morning in the small town of Kairana, Zainab watched her Ammi move the sevaiyan from the tin to a glass bowl. Pankaj, from next door, was outside playing.

When he came in, Ammi said, "Pankaj, help yourself to sevaiyan."

Zainab whispered, "He'll look in the tin. He didn't see you move it."

Sure enough, Pankaj went straight to the empty tin. Zainab laughed and pointed at the bowl.

qa.q: Where did Ammi move the sevaiyan to?
qa.a: She moved it from the tin to a glass bowl.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel when Pankaj went to the empty tin?
qa.a: Zainab felt amused and pleased, laughing because she had guessed right.

qa.q: How could Ammi help Zainab keep thinking this way?
qa.a: Ask her why Pankaj would look in the tin and praise her explanation.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have felt finding the tin empty?
qa.a: Pankaj may have felt confused or disappointed until Zainab pointed to the bowl.

grounding: On Eid, a child understands that a neighbour will wrongly believe the sweets are still in the tin because he didn't see them moved.

passage:
On Christmas Eve in Johannesburg, Gogo hid the presents in the hall cupboard. Zanele, five, peeked and then moved one present under her bed to keep it safe.

Her cousin Sofia asked, "Where will Gogo look for your present?"

Zanele thought. "In the cupboard. That's where she put it. She doesn't know I moved it."

Sofia giggled. "She'll be so confused!"

Zanele ran to tell Gogo before she could worry.

qa.q: Where did Zanele move the present?
qa.a: She moved one present under her bed.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when she ran to tell Gogo?
qa.a: Zanele was caring and a little worried, wanting to tell Gogo before she became confused.

qa.q: How could an adult build on Zanele's thinking?
qa.a: Ask her more "where will they look" questions in play, like hiding toys when someone is out of the room.

qa.q: What was it like for Sofia to hear Zanele's answer?
qa.a: Sofia found it funny, giggling at how confused Gogo would be.

grounding: At Christmas, a child understands that her grandmother believes the present is still where she hid it.

passage:
On a rainy morning at the nursery school, Dolma Ma'am put her umbrella in the stand and went to the office.

While she was away, the helper moved all the umbrellas to the bathroom to drip.

Tanvir watched. When Ma'am came back looking for her umbrella, he ran up. "You think it's in the stand, but it's not! Didi moved it."

Dolma Ma'am smiled. "How did you know I'd look there?"

qa.q: Where did the helper move the umbrellas?
qa.a: The helper moved all the umbrellas to the bathroom to drip.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when he ran up to Dolma Ma'am?
qa.a: Tanvir was excited and eager to help, sure he knew something she didn't.

qa.q: How can Dolma Ma'am build on Tanvir's understanding?
qa.a: She can ask him to explain how he knew, which helps him put his thinking into words.

qa.q: How might Dolma Ma'am feel about Tanvir's help?
qa.a: Dolma Ma'am was pleased and curious about how he understood her mistake.

grounding: On a rainy day at nursery, a child understands that his teacher still believes her umbrella is in the stand.

passage: I'm Devika, Akash's didi. It was Makar Sankranti, and Ma had filled the old laddoo tin with kite string. Akash opened it, frowned at the string, and shut it. When Dadu came in, I asked Akash, "What will Dadu think is inside?" He grinned. "Laddoos! But it's string. He'll be wrong." Dadu opened it and groaned. Akash rolled on the floor laughing. Last year he'd have said "string". I don't know exactly what changed in his head, but something did.

qa.q: What had Ma filled the old laddoo tin with?
qa.a: She had filled it with kite string.

qa.q: Why did Akash grin before Dadu opened the tin?
qa.a: He was delighted to know something Dadu didn't, expecting Dadu to think it held laddoos.

qa.q: How could the family keep encouraging this kind of thinking?
qa.a: They could play guessing games about what others know, like asking "What does Ma think is in the box?" before revealing it.

qa.q: What is it like for Dadu to open the tin?
qa.a: Dadu expects a sweet and finds string, so is disappointed for a moment, though the joke brings the family laughing together. 😄

grounding: Shows a young child understanding that his grandfather will wrongly believe a tin holds sweets.
